Content:
The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality (sometimes called the Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz Inequality) provides a connection between dot products and norms. It states that for any two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{u}] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}] in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n], we have the inequality
[MATH: \vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.]

Content:
In other words, the absolute value of the dot product is no more than the product of the norms.

Content:
For instance, if [MATH: [3; − 4]] and [MATH: [5; 12]] then
[MATH: |u ⋅ v||≤ ‖u‖ ⋅ ‖v‖;|3 ⋅ 5 + (− 4) ⋅ 12||≤ sqrt(3^{2} + (− 4)^{2})sqrt(5^{2} + 12^{2});|− 33||≤ 5 ⋅ 13; 33|≤ 65.✓]

Content:
Note: An easy trick to remember the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is to think of the formula for the dot product:
[MATH: \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta]
Because [MATH: \vert \cos \theta \vert \leq 1,] we can see that
[MATH: \vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.]

Content:
Watch out! The above trick is only a mnemonic trick, not an actual proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The formula [MATH: \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta] is actually a consequence of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, so a proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality cannot use the formula.

Content:
Now, using the dot product, we can define the acute angle [MATH: \theta] between two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{u}] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}] in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n], where [MATH: n \ge 2].

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/108f7904606dade0406336d5988db3f2]

Content:
To do that, we say that [MATH: \cos\theta] will be equal to the ratio of the two sides of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \cos\theta	=	\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert}]

Content:
Notice that this formula is completely analogous to the formula for the angle between two vectors in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space. It only works for non-zero vectors (otherwise, we will be dividing by zero).

Content:
Since the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality guarantees that [MATH: |\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq \| \mathbf{u} \| \cdot \| \mathbf{v} \|], we get
[MATH: -1 \leq \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert} \leq 1,]
which means that [MATH: \theta] can be found given any two non-zero [MATH: \mathbf{u}] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}].

Using the formula

[MATH: \cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{w}}{\Vert\mathbf{v}\Vert \, \Vert \mathbf{w}\Vert},]

we have the following:

[MATH: \cos θ|= (v_{1}w_{1} + v_{2}w_{2} + v_{3}w_{3} + v_{4}w_{4})/(sqrt(v_{1}^{2} + v_{2}^{2} + v_{3}^{2} + v_{4}^{2})sqrt(w_{1}^{2} + w_{2}^{2} + w_{3}^{2} + w_{4}^{2})); = ((− 1) ⋅ (− 2) + 2 ⋅ 2 + (− 4) ⋅ (− 2) + (− 2) ⋅ 2)/(sqrt((− 1)^{2} + 2^{2} + (− 4)^{2} + (− 2)^{2})sqrt((− 2)^{2} + 2^{2} + (− 2)^{2} + 2^{2})); = (10)/(sqrt(25) ⋅ sqrt(16)); = (10)/(5 ⋅ 4); = (1)/(2)]

Therefore,

[MATH: \theta=\arccos \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality (sometimes called the Cauchy-Bunyakovsky-Schwarz Inequality) provides a connection between dot products and norms. It states that for any two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{u}] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}] in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n], we have the inequality
[MATH: \vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.]

Content:
In other words, the absolute value of the dot product is no more than the product of the norms.

Content:
For instance, if [MATH: [3; − 4]] and [MATH: [5; 12]] then
[MATH: |u ⋅ v||≤ ‖u‖ ⋅ ‖v‖;|3 ⋅ 5 + (− 4) ⋅ 12||≤ sqrt(3^{2} + (− 4)^{2})sqrt(5^{2} + 12^{2});|− 33||≤ 5 ⋅ 13; 33|≤ 65.✓]

Content:
Note: An easy trick to remember the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is to think of the formula for the dot product:
[MATH: \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta]
Because [MATH: \vert \cos \theta \vert \leq 1,] we can see that
[MATH: \vert \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.]

Content:
Watch out! The above trick is only a mnemonic trick, not an actual proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The formula [MATH: \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v = \Vert \mathbf u \Vert \Vert \mathbf v \Vert \cos \theta] is actually a consequence of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, so a proof of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality cannot use the formula.

---

Item 2 — Example: Determining a Minimum Possible Value Using the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality

Example Prompt:
Consider the vector [MATH: [1; sqrt(k); − 2; 1]] Given that [MATH: \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}=-12] and [MATH: \Vert \mathbf{v}\Vert =4,] what is the smallest possible value of [MATH: k?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We will use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

[MATH: \vert \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.]

We are given all the quantities in the inequality above, except for [MATH: \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert.] So first, we compute [MATH: \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert] as follows:

[MATH: ‖u‖|= sqrt(1^{2} + (sqrt(k))^{2} + (− 2)^{2} + 1^{2}); = sqrt(6 + k)]

Now, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

[MATH: |u ⋅ v||≤ ‖u‖ ⋅ ‖v‖;|− 12||≤ sqrt(6 + k) ⋅ (4); 12|≤ 4sqrt(6 + k); 3|≤ sqrt(6 + k); 3^{2}|≤ (sqrt(6 + k))^{2}; 9|≤ 6 + k; 3|≤ k.]

Therefore, the smallest possible value of [MATH: k] is [MATH: 3.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Angle Between Two Vectors

Content:
Now, using the dot product, we can define the acute angle [MATH: \theta] between two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{u}] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}] in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n], where [MATH: n \ge 2].

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/108f7904606dade0406336d5988db3f2]

Content:
To do that, we say that [MATH: \cos\theta] will be equal to the ratio of the two sides of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \cos\theta	=	\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert}]

Content:
Notice that this formula is completely analogous to the formula for the angle between two vectors in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space. It only works for non-zero vectors (otherwise, we will be dividing by zero).

Content:
Since the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality guarantees that [MATH: |\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq \| \mathbf{u} \| \cdot \| \mathbf{v} \|], we get
[MATH: -1 \leq \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert} \leq 1,]
which means that [MATH: \theta] can be found given any two non-zero [MATH: \mathbf{u}] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}].

---

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Acute Angle Between Two Vectors

Example Prompt:
Find the acute angle between the vectors [MATH: [− 1; 2; − 4; − 2]] and [MATH: [− 2; 2; − 2; 2]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the formula

[MATH: \cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{w}}{\Vert\mathbf{v}\Vert \, \Vert \mathbf{w}\Vert},]

we have the following:

[MATH: \cos θ|= (v_{1}w_{1} + v_{2}w_{2} + v_{3}w_{3} + v_{4}w_{4})/(sqrt(v_{1}^{2} + v_{2}^{2} + v_{3}^{2} + v_{4}^{2})sqrt(w_{1}^{2} + w_{2}^{2} + w_{3}^{2} + w_{4}^{2})); = ((− 1) ⋅ (− 2) + 2 ⋅ 2 + (− 4) ⋅ (− 2) + (− 2) ⋅ 2)/(sqrt((− 1)^{2} + 2^{2} + (− 4)^{2} + (− 2)^{2})sqrt((− 2)^{2} + 2^{2} + (− 2)^{2} + 2^{2})); = (10)/(sqrt(25) ⋅ sqrt(16)); = (10)/(5 ⋅ 4); = (1)/(2)]

Therefore,

[MATH: \theta=\arccos \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.]

Item 9 — Example: Calculating the Cosine of an Angle

[MATH: a = OA^(→) = [− 2; 4; − 2; 2], b = OB^(→) = [4; 0; − 1; − 4].]

Also, let [MATH: \theta = m\angle{AOB}] be the angle between the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}.] Then, we can find [MATH: \cos \theta] using the formula:

[MATH: \cos θ|= (a ⋅ b)/(‖a‖‖b‖); = (a_{1}b_{1} + a_{2}b_{2} + a_{3}b_{3} + a_{4}b_{4})/(sqrt(a_{1}^{2} + a_{2}^{2} + a_{3}^{2} + a_{4}^{2})sqrt(b_{1}^{2} + b_{2}^{2} + b_{3}^{2} + b_{4}^{2})); = ((− 2) ⋅ 4 + 4 ⋅ 0 + (− 2) ⋅ (− 1) + 2 ⋅ (− 4))/(sqrt((− 2)^{2} + 4^{2} + (− 2)^{2} + 2^{2})sqrt(4^{2} + 0^{2} + (− 1)^{2} + (− 4)^{2}))); = (− 14)/(sqrt(28) ⋅ sqrt(33)); = (− 14)/(sqrt(14) ⋅ sqrt(2) ⋅ sqrt(33)); = − (sqrt(14))/(sqrt(2) ⋅ sqrt(33)); = − sqrt((7)/(33))]
